title: Is a flagship phone store on Durbar Marg worth the rent?

fields.Primer: A retailer weighs a premium-phone flagship / Demand is unknown but rent is fixed / Defend a monthly range and a sign-or-not call.
fields.Scenario and goal: Leadership wants a lease decision this week. Goal pin: does monthly demand cover the break-even of 125 phones?
fields.Artifacts: R A1 Kathmandu district population 2,041,587 (S14). S A2 store economics: fixed cost NPR 1,500,000/month; margin NPR 12,000 per phone; break-even 125. S A3 locked 1: premium-buyer replacement cycle about 3 years. S A4 locked 2: a single flagship typically captures 3% to 8% of area premium buyers.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ (unit = phones per month; why segment before applying a rate; what a replacement cycle does to monthly demand) → Clarify (time window; capture share) → Logic path choice (population→adults→premium→cycle→capture / flat 1% / count competitors) → Dials (adults, premium share, cycle, capture) → Pushback if capture > 8% or premium > 12% → Decision claim (sign / pilot / do not sign) → Reflect.
fields.Trap: Top-down shortcut → choosing "flat 1% of population" at the logic-path step.
fields.Defensible: P1 sign if capture ≥ 4.2% is credible (accepts rent risk); P2 pilot or shorter lease first (accepts delay); P3 shop-in-shop instead (accepts weaker brand control).
fields.Reference trace: 2,041,587 × 65% = 1.33M adults; × 8% = 106k premium; ÷ 3 years ÷ 12 = 2,950/month; capture 5% = about 148 vs break-even 125 (1.18×); break-even capture = 125 ÷ 2,950 = 4.2%; range 89 to 236.
fields.Pump: "Replace one flat rate with a chain of two or three observable rates, then check which link moves the decision most."
fields.Retry seeds: rent and margin vary (NPR 1.2M to 1.8M; margin NPR 11k to 13k). Optional conflicting-source card (S15) shows two household device-access figures that define "phone" differently; resolution: use premium-segment share, not device access.

title: How many Quick Pay uses per week should we buy capacity for?

fields.Primer: A payments feature launches next month / Demand depends on who can use it / Defend one contract tier.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM for a finance app launching "Quick Pay". Goal: choose the payment-partner tier (Tier S up to 30,000 uses/week; Tier L up to 100,000/week with a higher minimum).
fields.Artifacts: S A1 1.2M monthly active users; weekly actives are 55% of MAU. S A2 locked 1: 35% of weekly actives transact in-app each week. S A3 locked 2: last two feature launches reached 4% and 6% adoption in 30 days. S A4 tier price sheet.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ (correct denominator for adoption; difference between users and uses; why 30-day adoption is not steady state) → Clarify the audience → Decomposition by activity level (heavy/medium/light transactors) → Dials (adoption, uses per user per week = 1.8) → Pushback if adoption > 9% ("last launches reached 4–6%") → Decision.
fields.Trap: Wrong-denominator trap → applying adoption to all MAU.
fields.Defensible: P1 Tier S with an upgrade clause (accepts a capacity-breach risk); P2 Tier L if the user argues adoption above 7.2% with evidence (accepts paying for unused capacity).
fields.Reference trace: 1.2M × 55% = 660k; × 35% = 231k transactors; at 12% adoption = 27.7k users × 1.8 = 49.9k uses/week; at 5% = 11.6k × 1.8 = 20.8k. Tier S suffices while adoption ≤ 30,000 ÷ (1.8 × 231,000) = 7.2%.
fields.Pump: "Name the population before you name the rate; the denominator decides the order of magnitude."

title: How many support agents for launch-day chat?

fields.Primer: A help chat launches inside the app / Chats are not people; agents handle several at once / Defend a staffing number.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM launching in-app help chat. Goal: staffing for launch day without long queues.
fields.Artifacts: S A1 400,000 daily active users. S A2 locked 1: 0.6% of daily actives contact support on a normal day; launch week runs 1.5× normal; 70% of contacts choose chat. S A3 locked 2: average handle time 9 minutes; each agent handles 3 chats at once; 80% occupancy; 8-hour shift. S A4 locked 2: 40% of chats arrive in the 3 busiest hours.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ (concurrency vs handle time; what occupancy means; why peaks matter) → Decomposition (volume → workload minutes → agents; or volume → peak-hour → agents) → Dials → Pushback if peak ignored → Decision (a staffing range and a trigger to add agents).
fields.Trap: Unit-mixing → dividing chats per day by chats per agent without concurrency and occupancy.
fields.Defensible: P1 staff to the peak hour (about 21 agents) with flex; P2 staff to the daily workload (about 20) plus on-call surge pool; each accepts overstaff vs queue risk.
fields.Pump: "Convert counts into workload minutes before dividing by capacity."

title: Rainstorm in New York: how many extra drivers to incentivise?

fields.Primer: Rain raises demand and slows every trip / Normal-day productivity no longer holds / Defend an extra-driver number that keeps waits under 10 minutes.
fields.Scenario and goal: Ops PM at a ride-hail app. A storm hits the Manhattan core at 6 pm. Goal: keep average wait under 10 minutes by incentivising driver supply.
fields.Artifacts: R A1 NYC high-volume FHV trips Jan 2026: 22,108,438 (about 713k/day) (S13). R A2 average citywide wait 5.4 min (S13). S A3 core zone gets 35% of trips; the evening peak hour is 7% of a day; each driver completes 1.6 trips/hour normally. S A4 CONFLICT: traffic API says speeds fall 35%; fleet telematics says 20% (resolution: telematics sample is highway-heavy; use the midpoint ≈ 27% for city streets) locked 2. S A5 locked 2: past storms raised requests +35% to +55% (mean +42%); surge priced at 1.8× cut requests 18–25%. S A6 locked 2: 8% of drivers log off in heavy rain.
fields.Run: Branch: which constraint binds first (demand surge / slower trips / driver exits) → Dials with sources → Calculator → Probe: "Your two speed sources disagree; which do you trust?" → Pushback if no demand-shaping lever considered ("incentives alone recruit only part of the need") → Decision: extra drivers plus two non-driver levers.
fields.Trap: Average-day trap → using 1.6 trips/hour and today's supply during the storm.
fields.Defensible: P1 incentivise about 2,600–3,000 drivers plus pooled-ride nudges and honest ETAs; P2 incentivise more (about 5,000+) and accept cost; P3 accept longer waits in outer zones to protect the core.
fields.Reference trace: baseline peak-hour trips in the zone = 713,175 × 7% × 35% = 17,473; drivers = 17,473 ÷ 1.6 = 10,921. Storm: requests × 1.42 = 24,812; surge cuts 22% → 19,353; speed −27% → trips per driver = 1.6 ÷ (1 ÷ 0.73) = 1.17; drivers after exits = 10,921 × 0.92 = 10,047; need 19,353 ÷ 1.17 = 16,541; gap = 6,494. Incentives typically recruit 40% of the gap within 45 minutes ≈ 2,600; rest is demand-shaping and wait tolerance.
fields.Pump: "Re-derive every productivity rate under the shock; never reuse the normal-day rate."

title: Ticket on-sale: how fast should the waiting room admit fans?

fields.Primer: A show with 10,000 seats goes on sale at noon / Two teams disagree on demand and the payment limit is fixed / Defend an admission rate and a message to fans.
fields.Scenario and goal: Ticketing PM. Goal: sell out without payment failures or fans seeing a broken checkout.
fields.Artifacts: S A1 10,000 seats; 2 tickets per order on average. S A2 CONFLICT: marketing says 250,000 interested; CRM shows 60,000 verified fans (resolution: marketing counts all email opens; use verified fans × show-up rate 55% ≈ 33,000 arrivals, plus a bot allowance) locked 1. S A3 payment provider limit 40 authorisations/second; target ≤ 70% (28/s) locked 2. S A4 45% of admitted users attempt payment; 1.3 authorisation calls per attempt; 80% succeed locked 2. S A5 seat hold 5 minutes.
fields.Run: Branch: protect payment limit / protect fairness / protect speed → Dials → Probe: "A bot farm sends 40,000 requests; what do you change?" → Pushback if admit rate pushes authorisations over 28/s → Decision: admission rate, the message shown at queue positions beyond the likely sell-out point, and an anti-bot step.
fields.Trap: Average-day trap variant (treating arrival as steady rather than a spike; or sizing to marketing's 250,000).
fields.Defensible: P1 admit about 40–48/s with honest "sold out likely beyond position ~14,000" message; P2 lottery for fairness (accepts weaker demand-signal); P3 slower admit with longer hold (accepts a longer sell-out time).
fields.Reference trace: orders needed = 10,000 ÷ 2 = 5,000; orders per admitted user = 0.45 × 0.80 = 0.36; admitted needed = 5,000 ÷ 0.36 = 13,889; authorisations/s = admit/s × 0.45 × 1.3 = 0.585 × admit/s; max admit = 28 ÷ 0.585 = 47.9/s; sell-out time = 13,889 ÷ 47.9 = 290 s ≈ 4.8 minutes.
fields.Pump: "Find the binding limit first, then size everything else to it."

title: Tihar week: do we have enough riders for sweets and gifts?

fields.Primer: Festival demand compresses into two days / Last year's two numbers disagree / Defend a rider plan.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM at a delivery app in Kathmandu Valley. Goal: enough riders for festival gift orders without paying for idle capacity.
fields.Artifacts: R A1 Kathmandu district population 2,041,587; national average household size ≈ 4.4 (S14) → about 464,000 households. S A2 CONFLICT: ops dashboard shows 9,400 festival orders last year; finance shows 7,100 net of cancellations (24.5% cancelled; resolution: finance excludes cancelled orders; plan capacity on gross) locked 1. S A3 growth +35% year on year locked 2. S A4 60% of orders fall in two peak days; 55% of a day's orders land in a 4-hour window locked 2. S A5 a rider completes 2.2 orders/hour in festival traffic; normal active riders at that hour 600, down 35% in festival week locked 2.
fields.Run: Branch: top-down (households × adoption) vs bottom-up (last year × growth) → Dials → Triangulate (the two routes must be reconciled) → Probe: "Your top-down gives 19,500 orders; last year plus growth gives about 12,700. Which do you trust?" → Pushback → Decision: riders to guarantee, cap rules for peak slots.
fields.Trap: Single-route trap (committing to one unchecked estimate).
fields.Defensible: P1 calibrate to ~13,000 orders and guarantee about 60–80 riders as a buffer; P2 plan for 19,500 and over-staff; P3 cap slots and shift delivery windows.
fields.Reference trace: top-down at 3% share: 464k × 3% × 1.4 = 19.5k; calibrated at 2%: 9,280 households × 1.4 = 13.0k vs bottom-up 9,400 × 1.35 = 12.7k. Peak: 13.0k × 60% ÷ 2 = 3.9k/day; × 55% = 2,145 per 4 hours = 536/hour → riders needed 536 ÷ 2.2 = 244 vs supply 600 × 0.65 = 390 (1.6×). At 19.5k the need would be 366 vs 390 (1.07×), so the decision flips on calibration.
fields.Pump: "Estimate twice by two routes; resolve the gap before committing."

title: Terminal outage: where do 60 manual agents go?

fields.Primer: Check-in systems fail and the terminal must run manually / Every stage depends on the stage before it / Defend where limited staff go.
fields.Scenario and goal: Duty PM at a simulated airport terminal (inspired by the September 2025 check-in outages at European airports, S22; all numbers simulated). Goal: maximise passengers who depart within three hours without a terminal gridlock.
fields.Artifacts: S A1 next 3 hours: 36 departures, 7,200 passengers; 55% already hold a boarding pass; 3,240 need manual check-in; 60% have bags (1,944). S A2 60 agents; 12 passengers per agent-hour (check-in plus bag tag) → 720/hour; 2,160 in 3 hours (66.7% of need). S A3 security cap 2,400/hour. S A4 bag-drop closes at departure −60 min; gate closes −20 min; manual boarding takes about 2× as long (gates open 20 min earlier). S A5 locked 2: 20 retail and ground staff could be trained in 40 minutes (taking them away costs those desks). S A6 locked 2: flight clusters: peak hour holds 3,100 passengers.
fields.Run: Branch 1: allocate agents across (early flights / late flights / assisted passengers) → Branch 2: security staging → Branch 3: staff training or not → PIVOT: "Security throughput drops to 1,800/hour; the fast lane relied on the same system" → Probe 1: "Why move agents from check-in?" → Probe 2: "Which flights do you hold on the ground?" → Pushback if capacity > 100% assumed → Decision: allocation, holds, comms, kill criteria.
fields.Trap: Isolated-variable trap → optimising check-in only while security becomes the binding stage.
fields.Defensible: P1 re-allocate agents to security and boarding assist after the pivot and ground-hold the latest flights; P2 keep check-in strong and add paper-pass priority for tight connections; P3 request a controlled departure slot shift (accepts airline cost).
fields.Reference trace: serial stages: check-in 720/h, security 2,400/h, then 1,800/h after the pivot; 3 hours × 1,800 = 5,400 of 7,200 passengers (75%), so about 9 of 36 flights cannot clear security in the window whatever check-in does; agents beyond the check-in need of 3,240 passengers do not help; the binding stage becomes security.
fields.Pump: "Name every serial stage and its capacity before assigning scarce people to any of them."

title: Results day: web, SMS or phone, which will break first?

fields.Primer: Exam results go live at 10:00 / If one channel slows, people move to another / Defend where to spend 48 hours of engineering.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM at an exam authority (fictional) publishing national results. Goal: no channel collapse in the first 30 minutes.
fields.Artifacts: S A1 480,000 students; 70% check in the first 30 minutes (336,000). S A2 web capacity 2,000 requests/second; each visit makes 6 requests. S A3 SMS gateway 150 messages/second; retries double the load. S A4 phone lines 400; average call 90 seconds. S A5 locked 2: if web latency exceeds 5 seconds, 40% of users switch to SMS and 15% to phone. S A6 locked 2: a static lookup page on a CDN can serve results from sharded files (no database). S A7 locked 3: ministry insists on one simultaneous release.
fields.Run: Branch 1: predict first failure (web / SMS / phone) → Branch 2: allocate effort (static results shards / SMS throttling / phone deflection / communications) → PIVOT: "Ministry insists on exactly 10:00 for everyone; the staged release is cancelled" → Probe: "What do you tell people whose SMS is delayed?" → Probe: "What do you cut if you lose two engineers?" → Pushback → Decision: sequence, monitoring thresholds, and public messaging.
fields.Trap: Isolated-variable trap → fixing the web channel and ignoring where the overflow lands.
fields.Defensible: P1 static CDN lookup so most users never touch the origin, plus SMS rate-limit and queue; P2 staged release by roll-number range (accepts political friction); P3 cap SMS to one result per number and deflect phone entirely.
fields.Reference trace: average = 336,000 ÷ 1,800 = 187 users/s; first-minutes peak ≈ 3× = 560/s; web load = 560 × 6 = 3,360 req/s vs 2,000 (1.68× over); overflow to SMS = 40% × 560 = 224/s (retries make about 450/s) vs 150/s; phone 15% × 560 = 84 calls/s vs 400 ÷ 90 = 4.4 calls/s. Phone cannot absorb overflow; web overload cascades into SMS then phone.
fields.Pump: "Trace where each failure sends its users before you decide what to harden."

title: The festival exodus: charging capacity on a highway corridor

fields.Primer: Thousands of EVs leave the city in one day / The grid connection, not the number of chargers, sets the limit / Defend a policy for who charges, when and for how long.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM for a charging network (simulated). Goal: maximise served sessions on the peak day without queues that make drivers abandon.
fields.Artifacts: S A1 a corridor station with 10 fast chargers (120 kW each) on a 1.2 MW grid connection. S A2 locked 1: 1,800 EVs pass in the 10-hour peak; 35% need a charge (630 sessions); average 30 kWh. S A3 locked 2: waits above 40 minutes make 50% of drivers skip the station. S A4 locked 2: a 500 kWh rentable battery pack adds about 17 sessions. S A5 locked 2: pricing by time of day can shift 15% of sessions to off-peak. S A6 locked 3: grid upgrade quote: 9 months.
fields.Run: Branch 1: more chargers vs session-energy cap vs reservations → Branch 2: pricing → PIVOT: "Two chargers go offline (power sharing now caps at 8 chargers × 120 kW = 960 kW)" → Probe: "Why not just add chargers?" → Probe: "Who loses when you cap sessions at 20 kWh?" → Pushback → Decision with kill-criteria and communication.
fields.Trap: Isolated-variable trap → adding chargers when the grid limit binds.
fields.Defensible: P1 cap sessions at ~20 kWh with reservations and off-peak incentives; P2 rent a battery pack and add time-of-day pricing; P3 accept lower service and publish honest wait times.
fields.Reference trace: energy needed = 630 × 30 = 18.9 MWh; energy available = 1.2 MW × 10 h = 12 MWh (63%); max sessions at 30 kWh = 400; at 20 kWh = 600 (95% of 630); after the pivot: 0.96 MW × 10 h = 9.6 MWh = 320 sessions at 30 kWh or 480 at 20 kWh. Adding chargers raises nothing once power is shared.
fields.Pump: "Compare energy needed with energy deliverable before touching any other variable."

title: Sign-ups dropped 12% after the app update

fields.Primer: A key metric fell right after a release / The cheapest check is whether the number is even real / Defend your first action.
fields.Scenario and goal: StreamNest (fictional subscription streamer; practice context Netflix-style) saw weekly sign-ups fall 12% the week after app v7.4. Goal: decide whether to roll back the UI.
fields.Artifacts: S dashboard: client event "signup_complete" 41,000 → 36,080 (−12%). Locked cards: E1(1) server-side billing sign-ups 40,600 → 40,900 (flat); E2(1) by platform (client events): iOS 17,000 → 17,100; Android 17,500 → 12,580 (−28%); Web 6,500 → 6,400; E3(1) Android by app version/OS: event fire-rate 99% → 61% on Android 14 devices running v7.4; E4(2) release notes: analytics SDK upgraded in v7.4; E5(2) competitor promotions: none (red herring); E6(2) funnel tap-through on new UI: unchanged (red herring).
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ (client vs server metric; what a segment is; why verify before fixing) → clarify metric/timeframe → evidence → rank hypotheses (tracking bug / UI regression / seasonality / competitor) → diagnosis → next action.
fields.Trap: Hypothesis trap → choosing "roll back the UI" before verifying the metric.
fields.Defensible: P1 do not roll back; hotfix tracking; add a client-versus-server reconciliation alert; P2 pause the staged rollout expansion for 24 hours while verifying (accepts a short delay).
fields.Reference trace: server-side flat → the loss is in measurement, not users; Android −28% while iOS flat points to a platform-specific event failure; fire-rate 61% on one OS confirms; cost 3 tokens.
fields.Pump: "Compare two independent measures of the same event before assuming behavior changed."
fields.Retry seeds: affected OS and size of drop vary; a seed where the server-side number also falls.

title: New seller activations fell 15%

fields.Primer: A funnel shrank without any visible change / The loss is at one step / Defend where you look first.
fields.Scenario and goal: SellMate (fictional marketplace) weekly new-seller activations fell from 12,000 to 10,200 (−15%). Goal: find the broken step and pick a fix.
fields.Artifacts: S funnel: 30,000 starts/week (flat) × phone-verify completion 62.0% → 52.7% × listing completion 64.5% (flat). Locked: E1(1) funnel by step: only "verify phone" fell; E2(1) verify completion by carrier: A 71% → 70%, B 60% → 31%, C 52% → 51% (starts: A 40%, B 30%, C 30%); E3(2) SMS vendor delivery logs: carrier B delivery rate 96% → 41%; E4(1) by device/OS: flat (red herring); E5(1) app releases in window: none; E6(2) listing quality: flat (red herring).
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ → clarify → evidence → rank → diagnosis (single point of failure) → next action (restore verification for carrier B; success measure).
fields.Trap: Hypothesis trap → blaming the onboarding UI or pricing.
fields.Defensible: P1 route carrier B through a backup SMS provider; P2 offer voice or email verification fallback temporarily; P3 both (accepts higher fraud exposure with email-only).
fields.Reference trace: weighted verify completion: before 0.4×71 + 0.3×60 + 0.3×52 = 62.0; after 0.4×70 + 0.3×31 + 0.3×51 = 52.6; the drop is carrier B only.
fields.Pump: "Slice by the dimension that explains where the step fails, not by the one that is easiest to pull."
fields.Retry seeds: carrier shares and which carrier fails.

title: Add-to-cart conversion fell after the layout refresh

fields.Primer: Overall conversion fell 9% after a redesign / Most segments look fine / Defend what you check second.
fields.Scenario and goal: CartWise (fictional retailer) search-to-cart conversion fell from 4.00% to 3.64%. Goal: find the segment and decide on a targeted fix.
fields.Artifacts: S device mix and conversion: phone 50% (3.6% → 3.6%), desktop 25% (5.0% → 5.0%), tablet 25% (3.8% → 2.36%). Locked: E1(1) by device (above); E2(1) tablet by orientation: portrait (40% of tablet) 3.8% → 3.8%; landscape (60%) 3.8% → 1.4%; E3(2) scroll depth: median scroll to the add-to-cart button 0.9 → 1.6 screens on tablet landscape; E4(2) 5% holdout on the old layout: tablet landscape 3.7%; E5(1) search relevance: unchanged (red herring); E6(2) payment errors: flat (red herring).
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ → clarify → evidence → rank → diagnosis → next action (targeted hotfix vs full rollback vs test).
fields.Trap: Hypothesis trap → blaming search relevance.
fields.Defensible: P1 hotfix a sticky add-to-cart bar for tablet landscape; P2 roll back the layout for tablet landscape only; P3 keep the layout and run a test (accepts continuing loss).
fields.Reference trace: 0.5×3.6 + 0.25×5.0 + 0.25×2.36 = 3.64; tablet landscape carries the whole drop; button pushed below the fold.
fields.Pump: "Keep slicing until one segment explains the whole change."

title: Search conversion fell while crash rates spiked

fields.Primer: Two alarms are ringing at once / The louder one may not be the bigger one / Defend which problem gets the first fix.
fields.Scenario and goal: ShopSphere (fictional marketplace; practice context Amazon-style) saw overall conversion fall from 3.20% to 3.00% while the crash rate rose. Goal: find the main driver of revenue loss and sequence the fixes.
fields.Artifacts: S locked cards: E1(1) crash-affected sessions 0.4% → 2.1% of sessions; E2(2) cohort split: crash-affected conversion 0.8%; non-crash conversion 3.05% (was 3.20%); E3(2) zero-result searches 2.1% → 9.4% of queries; sessions with ≥1 zero-result convert 1.1% vs 3.4% without; E4(1) deploy log: search index v18 Tuesday (stale inventory sync); SDK update Wednesday; E5(2) revenue decomposition: crashes explain about 25% of the conversion drop, search about 75%; E6(1) traffic mix and pricing: flat (red herrings).
fields.Run: Branch 1: rank hypotheses → evidence → cohort comparison (users who did not crash) → PROBE "The crash graph is the one leadership is watching; why not fix it first?" → PUSHBACK if search is ranked below crash without cohort evidence → diagnosis with sequencing.
fields.Trap: Loudest-signal trap → fixating on crash rate.
fields.Defensible: P1 repair search first, hotfix crashes in parallel; P2 hotfix crashes first because it is a 4-hour fix, then search (accepts delaying the larger lever by hours); both need the cohort comparison.
fields.Reference trace: crash share of drop = 2.1% × (3.20 − 0.80) = 0.050 of 0.20 points (25%); non-crash sessions explain the rest (0.979 × (3.20 − 3.047) = 0.15, 75%).
fields.Pump: "Compare users who experienced the loud problem with users who did not before assigning blame."
fields.Retry seeds: crash and zero-result magnitudes swap in one seed.

title: Delivery times rose three minutes yet every city got faster

fields.Primer: The average moved against the trend in each part / A new part joined the average / Defend what you will and will not change.
fields.Scenario and goal: DashRide (fictional delivery app). Average delivery time rose 30.4 → 33.4 minutes and refunds rose. Goal: decide whether to roll back recent platform changes.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(1) overall time 30.4 → 33.4; E2(1) by city: A 28 → 27; B 34 → 33; C (launched this quarter) 52; E3(2) order mix: before A 60%, B 40%; after A 50%, B 32%, C 18%; E4(2) refund rate by city: A 1.0%, B 1.2%, C 4.5% (overall 1.1% → 1.7%); E5(2) courier density: C 0.8 couriers per km² vs 2.1 and 1.9; E6(2) dispatch algorithm test (10% holdout): no difference (red herring).
fields.Run: Branch: confirm the metric, then cut by city → PROBE "Leadership wants the dispatch change rolled back; defend or reverse" → PUSHBACK if the aggregate average is used for the decision → diagnosis → next action.
fields.Trap: Loudest-signal trap (aggregate edition): trusting the blended average.
fields.Defensible: P1 keep the platform change; fix City C operations (courier incentives, tighter delivery radius); P2 pause marketing in City C until courier density improves; P3 add a mix-adjusted KPI for leadership.
fields.Pump: "Whenever an average moves, ask which groups entered or left it."
fields.Retry seeds: city shares and launch city size.

title: Daily users are up 8% but week-one retention is down

fields.Primer: Growth and retention disagree / A product change shipped the same week / Defend what caused each movement.
fields.Scenario and goal: Chirp (fictional social app). DAU +8%; day-7 retention 31.0% → 24.4%. Goal: decide whether to revert last week's feed-ranking change.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(1) retention by acquisition channel: organic 31% → 31%; promo channel 12%; E2(1) new-user mix: promo 0% → 35%; E3(2) feed-ranking experiment (10% holdout): D7 31.0% vs 30.8% (no difference); E4(1) notification volume: flat; E5(2) crash and latency: flat; E6(2) promo cost per install and quality notes.
fields.Run: Branch 1 rank hypotheses → evidence → PROBE "The feed change is the most recent; why not revert?" → PUSHBACK if acting before the channel split → diagnosis + next action.
fields.Trap: Loudest-signal trap → blaming the most recent product change.
fields.Defensible: P1 keep the feed change; report cohorts by channel; add a channel-quality guardrail; P2 cap the promo channel until onboarding for promo users is fixed.
fields.Pump: "Check who is in the metric before checking what changed in the product."

title: Drivers are leaving slowly in six cities

fields.Primer: A slow decline with several suspects / The system is working as designed / Defend a cause only after you have a control.
fields.Scenario and goal: RideKo (fictional ride-hail; practice context Uber-style). 90-day driver retention fell gradually over three months across six cities. A redesigned payout screen shipped to a random 50% of drivers. Goal: decide between a UI rollback and a deeper incentive change.
fields.Artifacts: S locked (10 tokens): E1(1) 90-day retention trend; E2(3) treatment vs control: control 61.0% → 58.9% (−2.1); treatment 61.2% → 55.6% (−5.6); E3(2) competitor bonus cities (one third of drivers): control −3.4; other cities control −1.45; E4(1) fuel price index +11%: affects all; E5(1) support tickets "where is my bonus": 3× in treatment; E6(2) treatment drivers who opened the earnings-detail tab: −3.0 vs −7.4 who did not (selection bias warning); E7(1) tenure mix: flat.
fields.Run: Branch 1 hypotheses → Branch 2 evidence path → PIVOT "The control group's data shows a 3-week lag in the competitor cities" → PROBE "How do you separate competitor effect from the screen?" → PROBE "Roll back or restructure?" → PUSHBACK on causal claims without control → decision with success measure.
fields.Trap: Convenient-cause trap → blaming the latest change (or the competitor) without a control.
fields.Defensible: P1 fix the screen to show bonus accrual in real time and add a targeted incentive in the two competitor cities; P2 roll back the screen as a safe baseline while redesigning; P3 restructure incentives so bonus appears in the trip view (accepts a bigger change).
fields.Reference trace: screen effect = −5.6 − (−2.1) = −3.5 points; competitor effect ≈ −3.4 − (−1.45) = −1.95 points in those cities; fuel is absorbed by the control baseline; the earnings-tab card is a clue, not proof.
fields.Pump: "Use the group that never saw the change to size the effect before choosing the fix."

title: Customer satisfaction is sliding while resolution times improve

fields.Primer: One metric improved and another decays slowly / Automation changed who reaches a human / Defend the cause and what you will not "fix".
fields.Scenario and goal: HelpDesk (fictional support platform). CSAT fell 4.44 → 4.26 over four months; resolution time improved 14.0 → 9.5 hours. A support bot launched in month two and reports 38% containment. Goal: diagnose and recommend.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(1) CSAT trend; E2(2) CSAT by complexity: simple 4.65 (stable), complex 3.70 (stable); E3(2) complex-ticket share 22% → 41%; E4(2) bot containment 38% reported; 30% of "contained" chats recontact within 48 hours; E5(2) new-agent cohort (under 90 days) CSAT 4.0 vs 4.5 (partial factor); E6(1) refund policy change: flat (red herring); E7(1) seasonal sale volume: modest.
fields.Run: Branch 1 hypotheses → Branch 2 evidence → PIVOT "Finance tells you the bot saves $210k per quarter; leadership wants it expanded" → PROBE "Do you switch the bot off?" → PROBE "What would you report instead of CSAT?" → decision.
fields.Trap: Convenient-cause trap → blaming agent training or the bot itself.
fields.Defensible: P1 keep the bot; report CSAT by complexity and recontact-adjusted containment; invest in complex-ticket handling; P2 narrow the bot's scope until recontact falls; P3 add a handoff-quality guardrail.
fields.Pump: "Check whether the group being measured changed before deciding the experience changed."
fields.Retry seeds: share of complex tickets and recontact rate.

title: Revenue per paying user is eroding by 7%

fields.Primer: A revenue ratio slides with four suspects / Some causes are healthy / Defend which to act on and which to leave alone.
fields.Scenario and goal: NoteWise (fictional SaaS). Average revenue per paying user (ARPPU) fell from $14.20 to $13.21 in five months. Goal: decide what to fix.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(1) ARPPU trend; E2(3) price-volume-mix decomposition: FX −$0.28; plan mix −$0.31; promotions −$0.25; seat contraction −$0.15 (sum −$0.99); E3(1) FX: two markets bill in EUR and GBP; E4(1) plan mix: annual share 22% → 34%; E5(2) 12-month retention: annual 84% vs monthly 61%; E6(2) promotion redemptions: legacy 40%-off code still active; E7(2) seat contraction: concentrated in teams over 20 seats.
fields.Run: Branch 1 hypotheses → Branch 2 evidence → PIVOT "The CFO wants ARPPU back to $14.20 by quarter end" → PROBE "Which of these causes is actually bad?" → PROBE "What metric replaces ARPPU?" → decision.
fields.Trap: Single-cause trap → treating every decline as a problem or naming one cause.
fields.Defensible: P1 act on promotion leakage and seat contraction; accept FX and annual-plan mix; P2 add a cohort-LTV view alongside ARPPU; P3 renegotiate currency pricing (accepts customer friction).
fields.Reference trace: 14.20 − 13.21 = 0.99 = 0.28 + 0.31 + 0.25 + 0.15; annual mix lowers ARPPU but raises retention (84% vs 61%), so it is partly healthy.
fields.Pump: "Decompose the movement into parts before judging whether it is good or bad."
fields.Retry seeds: component sizes; a seed where mix shift is harmful.

title: Students churn at re-verification: cut price or something else?

fields.Primer: A discounted tier loses members at one moment / More than one cause is hiding in the churn / Defend which lever you pull.
fields.Scenario and goal: Streamly (fictional music service; Spotify's published student rules, S23, are the real structure: up to 4 years, re-verify every 12 months, plan converts afterwards). Goal: raise revenue from the student tier.
fields.Artifacts: S student price $5.99 vs standard $11.99 (illustrative, not current Spotify pricing). S student base 1.0M. S churn by tenure: about 1.2% per month, spiking to 22% at the 12-month re-verification. S locked: E1(1) exit survey of re-verification churners: lapsed re-verification (could not or did not verify) 41%, price 24%, graduated 21%, switched service 14%; E2(2) test: a $4.99 price cut reduces spike churn by 2.5 points; E3(2) cost to serve and ARPU by tier; E4(1) competitor student pricing (similar).
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ (retention vs revenue, why timing of churn matters, what a segment-level lever is) → clarify the goal → evidence → options (cut price / add a value feature / smooth re-verification and add a graduation offer / do nothing) → decision with trade-off.
fields.Trap: Discount reflex → cutting price without testing which cause drives churn.
fields.Defensible: P1 fix re-verification friction (reminders, grace period) plus a graduation offer; P2 a value-add bundle with a test (accepts delay and build cost); P3 a targeted price cut only for price-cited churners (accepts leakage).
fields.Reference trace: spike churners = 220,000; lapsed re-verification = 41% = about 90,000; saving half = 45,000 users × $71.88/year = $3.24M with no price cost. Price cut to $4.99: 25,000 users saved × $59.88 = $1.50M, but 805,000 retained users × $12 = $9.66M lost.
fields.Pump: "Split the churn by cause before choosing a lever."
fields.Retry seeds: share of lapsed verification 25–50%; price elasticity.

title: When should the paywall appear?

fields.Primer: One decision, three timings / A high conversion rate can hide a small audience / Defend an overall result, not a flattering percentage.
fields.Scenario and goal: LinguaLoop (fictional language app). Goal: raise free-to-paid conversion with one lever: paywall timing.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(1) Day-1 paywall: shown to 100%; conversion 4.1%; D30 retention 18%; E2(1) After lesson 3: 62% reach it; conversion among them 9.0%; D30 retention 22%; E3(1) After a 7-day streak: 31% reach it; conversion among them 14.0%; E4(2) revenue per paid user is equal across options; E5(2) support cost differences: none.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ (conditional vs overall rate; denominator; what retention tells you) → clarify goal → evidence → decision with trade-off and a test plan.
fields.Trap: Generic growth answer → picking the highest conversion percentage (14.0%) without the audience size.
fields.Defensible: P1 after lesson 3 (overall 5.58%); P2 a hybrid: soft prompt at lesson 3, hard paywall after the streak (accepts complexity); P3 stay Day-1 for a revenue floor (accepts lower retention).
fields.Reference trace: overall conversion: Day-1 4.1%; lesson 3: 0.62 × 9.0% = 5.58%; streak: 0.31 × 14.0% = 4.34%.
fields.Pump: "Multiply the rate by the share of people who ever see it."

title: Raise the take rate for new sellers?

fields.Primer: A fee increase helps this quarter / Supply today is tomorrow's top sellers / Defend a fee decision with a number and a risk.
fields.Scenario and goal: BazaarKo (fictional marketplace). Goal: raise revenue by adjusting the take rate for new sellers from 10% to 12%.
fields.Artifacts: S competitor take rates 8%, 12%, 15%. S new sellers generate 18% of GMV. S locked: E1(1) a 2-point increase cut new-seller activation by 9% in a limited test; E2(2) 55% of top-5% sellers began in the last two years; E3(1) top 5% of sellers produce 40% of GMV; E4(2) seller survey: fee fairness ranks below payout speed.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ → clarify goal (this quarter vs year) → evidence → options (raise for all new / raise with tiers by GMV / keep and improve payout speed) → decision.
fields.Trap: Generic growth answer → raising fees because competitors charge more.
fields.Defensible: P1 tiered take rate (accepts complexity); P2 keep 10% for new sellers and add paid services (accepts slower revenue); P3 raise to 12% with a grace period for the first 90 days.
fields.Reference trace: baseline revenue = 0.82 × 10% + 0.18 × 10% = 10.0% of GMV; after: new-seller GMV 0.18 × 0.91 = 0.1638; revenue = 0.082 + 0.1638 × 12% = 10.17% of GMV (+1.7%). The gain is small against a pipeline risk (55% of tomorrow's top sellers are today's new sellers).
fields.Pump: "Put the gain and the long-term risk in the same units."

title: A rival adds a concierge: match, copy or pivot?

fields.Primer: A competitor changed the luxury offer / Demand data points two ways / Defend a position, not a reaction.
fields.Scenario and goal: StayLoft (fictional rental platform; practice context Airbnb-style). Luxury share fell from 31% to 28% in a quarter after a rival launched a curated concierge service. Goal: protect luxury profitability for the next year.
fields.Artifacts: S luxury is 22% of GMV; luxury bookings −4.5% quarter on quarter; S rival price premium +12%; rival NPS 62 vs ours 48; S locked: E1(2) search data: itinerary and concierge queries on luxury listings +60%; conversion from those searches 1.8% vs 3.1% overall; E2(2) cancellations 9.5% vs 6.1% a year ago; E3(2) unit economics: average luxury booking $2,400; take 14% = $336; concierge partner cost $85 per booking; test uplift in conversion +0.9 point; E4(2) host survey: 40% of top hosts would offer concierge-lite for a fee; E5(1) rival coverage: 6 destinations only.
fields.Run: Branch 1 goal clarification (share vs profit) → Branch 2 evidence order → Branch 3 position (match price / concierge layer / pivot segment) → PROBE "The rival covers six destinations; where do you not compete?" → PUSHBACK if copying the rival fully → decision.
fields.Trap: Copycat trap → matching the rival feature for feature.
fields.Defensible: P1 concierge-lite via hosts in the top destinations (accepts quality variance); P2 pivot to long-stay luxury (accepts smaller TAM); P3 hold price, fix cancellations first (accepts share loss).
fields.Reference trace: concierge adds $85 cost to a $336 take (25%); at a +0.9-point conversion uplift on a 1.8% base (+50% relative) the economics are favourable only in destinations where the rival is present; sequence by overlap.
fields.Pump: "Show why the lever works in this market, not just that it exists."
fields.Retry seeds: rival coverage and partner cost vary.

title: Launching a streamer where local telcos own distribution

fields.Primer: A global service enters a market with strong gatekeepers / Payment and language limit the obvious route / Defend a segment and a route to them.
fields.Scenario and goal: StreamNest (fictional) enters Country N. Goal: the clarification phase decides: raw subscriber growth or early profitability.
fields.Artifacts: S two telcos hold 88% of mobile subscriptions; S 18% of adults have a card, 62% use a mobile wallet; S 70% of viewing is local-language; S locked: E1(2) telco bundle wholesale ARPU $0.35/month vs direct price $2.00; E2(2) local competitor churn 6%/month; E3(2) piracy share of viewing 45%; E4(2) sports and local-film rights costs; E5(1) wallet integration time: 10 weeks; E6(2) price sensitivity test: $1 plan converts 3× the $2 plan.
fields.Run: Branch 1 goal → Branch 2 evidence order (what you pull first is scored) → Branch 3 route (telco bundle / wallet-direct mobile-only plan / local partner) → PROBE "A telco asks for exclusivity; do you accept?" → PUSHBACK on generic "localise and market" → decision with trade-off.
fields.Trap: Generic growth answer → "aggressive marketing and localisation".
fields.Defensible: P1 mobile-only wallet plan targeted at a segment, with a limited telco pilot; P2 telco bundle for reach (accepts low ARPU and dependence); P3 niche land grab in one language or genre (accepts small scale).
fields.Reference trace: telco route trades $2.00 for $0.35 (−82.5%) but removes the 18% card barrier; wallet route addresses 62%.
fields.Pump: "Name the constraint that makes your lever work here and nowhere else."
fields.Retry seeds: card and wallet shares; telco exclusivity terms.

title: An AI-native rival is winning the mid-market

fields.Primer: A new rival wins one tier of customers / The incumbent's strengths sit in another tier / Defend where to fight.
fields.Scenario and goal: TaskForge (fictional project-management SaaS). Mid-market win rate fell from 33% to 22% against an AI-native rival offering a free tier. Goal: protect growth for the next two quarters.
fields.Artifacts: S mid-market (10–200 seats): ARPA $9k, 46% of new ARR; enterprise ARPA $85k with a stable 41% win rate; S locked: E1(2) win/loss: 38% of lost deals cite price and AI automation; E2(2) integrations and compliance requirements appear in 70% of enterprise wins; E3(2) AI feature build: 4 months, $1.2M; E4(2) rival free tier converts 4% to paid; E5(1) our free-trial conversion 11%.
fields.Run: Branch 1 goal → Branch 2 evidence → Branch 3 position (build AI features broadly / unbundle a freemium tier / defend enterprise and moat) → PROBE "What if the free tier removes your price premium?" → decision.
fields.Trap: Copycat trap → feature parity chase.
fields.Defensible: P1 ship two targeted automations for the mid-market and defend enterprise; P2 freemium tier (accepts margin dilution); P3 retreat upmarket (accepts losing 46% of new ARR).
fields.Reference trace: expected new ARR at risk = 46% of new ARR; price-and-AI lost deals 38%; targeted automations cost less than the full build.
fields.Pump: "State what you will deliberately not build."

title: AI answers help users and starve publishers

fields.Primer: A feature that users like weakens the sources it relies on / Three pressures cannot all be satisfied / Defend a sequence and what you give up.
fields.Scenario and goal: AskLens (fictional search product; practice context Google-style). AI answers improve user satisfaction but reduce clicks to publishers. Goal: choose a strategy that balances user value, publisher health and regulatory pressure.
fields.Artifacts: R A1 Pew Research Center (S16): users clicked a traditional result in 8% of visits with an AI summary vs 15% without; clicked a cited source in 1% of visits; ended the session 26% vs 16% (the company in that study disputed the method). S internal: publisher referral traffic −18% on AI-answer queries; satisfaction +9 points; regulator inquiry opened. S locked: E1(2) high-value queries (health, finance, news) = 14% of volume but 40% of publisher revenue; E2(2) test: inline citation redesign raises source clicks from 1% to 4% at −1 point satisfaction; E3(2) licence-pool cost estimate; E4(2) throttled rollout lets you gather ecosystem data in 8 weeks; E5(3) regulator timeline: 6 months.
fields.Run: Branch 1 goal → Branch 2 evidence → PIVOT "A large publisher group threatens to block your crawler" → PROBE "What would make you limit AI answers?" → PROBE "Why not just pay?" → PUSHBACK on single-lever answers → decision with sequencing and kill-criteria.
fields.Trap: Ecosystem blindness (false binary: maximise answers or protect publishers).
fields.Defensible: P1 redesign citations plus limit AI answers on high-value queries; P2 throttle rollout and gather ecosystem data (accepts delay and regulator risk); P3 a licensing programme with usage-based payment (accepts cost).
fields.Reference trace: high-value queries are 14% of volume and 40% of publisher revenue, so limiting only there protects the most revenue with the smallest user-value loss; citations at 4% clicks are still far below the 15% non-AI baseline.
fields.Pump: "Show the sequence: which move buys information, which buys goodwill, which buys time."
fields.Retry seeds: share of high-value queries; regulator timeline.

title: A minimum-pay rule hits the biggest market

fields.Primer: A rule raises the cost of the core market / Every response changes demand, supply or politics / Defend a package, not a single move.
fields.Scenario and goal: RideKo (fictional) faces a minimum driver-pay rule in Country R (fictional) that raises cost per trip by 14%. Country R is 38% of revenue and 44% of profit. Goal: keep a viable business there.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(2) price elasticity −0.9; E2(2) driver supply responds to pay: +10% pay brings +6% supply; E3(2) rival Mobo is not yet subject to the rule; E4(2) low-density hours and zones lose money under the rule; E5(3) investors expect profit growth; E6(2) rider wait times already 6.5 minutes in suburbs.
fields.Run: Branch 1 goal → Branch 2 evidence → PIVOT "The rule extends to bonuses; incentive budgets now count toward the minimum" → PROBE "Do you raise fares 14%?" → PROBE "Which zones do you exit?" → decision with kill-criteria.
fields.Trap: False binary → "comply fully" vs "exit".
fields.Defensible: P1 partial fare rise, trim low-density service, reallocate incentives; P2 absorb cost for a year to defend share (accepts profit hit); P3 narrow service to the most profitable zones (accepts reach loss).
fields.Reference trace: a 14% cost rise passed through at elasticity −0.9 implies about −12.6% volume if fully passed to price; partial pass-through plus zone trimming balances profit and volume.
fields.Pump: "Compute the effect of each lever on volume and profit before ranking them."

title: A wallet's three growth paths all depend on one another

fields.Primer: Three attractive moves require each other / A fee cap shrinks the margin on all of them / Defend the order of moves.
fields.Scenario and goal: FinWallet (fictional super-app wallet). Goal: choose the next 12 months among lending, merchant payments and bill pay.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(2) merchant fee cap 0.5%; average merchant processes $2,400/month → $12 revenue; acquisition cost $38 → payback 3.2 months; E2(2) lending licence takes 9–12 months and needs merchant cash-flow data; E3(2) bill pay drives frequency (weekly use) but margin near zero; E4(2) partner bank concentration: 70% of float with one bank; E5(3) regulator may tighten wallet-to-wallet transfer rules; E6(2) churn of merchants without lending: 3%/month.
fields.Run: Branch 1 goal (growth vs profit) → Branch 2 evidence → PIVOT "The partner bank raises its fee by 30%" → PROBE "What do you stop doing?" → PROBE "How do you avoid depending on one bank?" → decision with sequence.
fields.Trap: False binary / ecosystem blindness → choosing one path in isolation.
fields.Defensible: P1 merchant payments first, bill pay as an acquisition hook, lending prepared on merchant data (sequenced); P2 bill pay first for frequency (accepts delayed profit); P3 apply for the lending licence immediately in parallel (accepts focus risk).
fields.Reference trace: payback 38 ÷ 12 = 3.2 months supports merchant acquisition; lending requires merchant data and 9–12 months, so the sequencing dependency drives the order.
fields.Pump: "Draw the dependency between moves; the order often matters more than the choice."

title: Live translation: three seconds or instant?

fields.Primer: A traveller needs a reply now / Quality and speed pull in opposite directions / Defend the choice and how you would prove it works.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM for a travel translation feature. Goal: pick the model setup for tourists in short conversations.
fields.Artifacts: S Model A (large): 94% semantic accuracy, 3.0 s median response. Model B (distilled): 88% accuracy, 0.4 s. S locked: E1(1) test with 40 tourists: sessions with replies slower than 1.5 s were abandoned 38% vs 9%; E2(1) phrase categories: menus and directions 80% of use; medical or pharmacy phrases 5%; E3(2) error severity: menus S3; directions S2; medical S1; E4(2) cost per 1,000 translations: A $1.80, B $0.30.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ (latency vs throughput; what a median hides; why error severity matters) → clarify user → component drop (A, B, or B plus verify-with-A for S1 categories) → define test (metric, threshold) → decision.
fields.Trap: Tech-first trap → choosing the large model because it is more accurate.
fields.Defensible: P1 B by default with a "double-check" action routed to A for S1 phrases; P2 B only with a clear accuracy disclaimer (accepts S1 exposure); P3 A with streaming partial output to hide latency (accepts cost).
fields.Reference trace: abandonment 38% vs 9% beyond 1.5 s; 88% accuracy on S2/S3 categories is acceptable; test: task-completion rate, repeat-ask rate, error-report rate; threshold: repeat-ask ≤ 15%.
fields.Pump: "Translate a user's patience into a latency number before choosing a model."

title: A shop assistant whose answers change hourly

fields.Primer: Stock levels change every hour / The assistant should talk like the brand / Defend how it gets its facts.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM for a retail chat assistant that answers "is this in stock at my store?". Goal: choose between retrieval and fine-tuning for stock facts.
fields.Artifacts: S fine-tune run costs $4,000 and takes 2 days; inventory changes every hour; S retrieval via the inventory API adds 250 ms and $0.002 per question; S locked: E1(1) brand tone guide exists (200 examples); E2(1) wrong-stock answers produce store visits that fail: complaint cost $6 per incident; E3(2) 15% of questions are about policy (returns), which changes monthly; E4(2) API reliability 99.5%.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ → clarify user need → component drop (retrieval for stock / fine-tune for tone / both) → define evaluation (accuracy on stock questions; stale-answer rate) → decision.
fields.Trap: Tech-first trap → fine-tuning facts that change faster than the training cycle.
fields.Defensible: P1 retrieval for stock and policy; light tone via system prompt; P2 small tone fine-tune plus retrieval (accepts cost); P3 retrieval with a fallback message when the API fails.
fields.Reference trace: stock changes hourly vs a 2-day fine-tune cycle → stale; retrieval gives fresh facts; evaluation: stale-answer rate < 1% on a 300-question set; fallback when API is down (0.5% of time).
fields.Pump: "Match how fast the fact changes to how fast the system can learn."

title: On-device or cloud for tagging kids' photos?

fields.Primer: Photos of children are sensitive / Phones differ widely in power / Defend where the model runs.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM for a family photo app adding auto-tagging. Goal: choose on-device or cloud inference.
fields.Artifacts: S cloud model 91% accuracy; on-device 82%; battery drain 3% per 100 photos on-device; older phones (30% of users) run it 4× slower; S locked: E1(1) survey: 71% of parents say they would not upload children's photos to a new cloud feature; E2(1) tag errors: wrong name tags rated annoying not harmful; E3(2) cloud cost $0.40 per 1,000 photos; E4(2) regulatory view: children's data triggers stricter consent rules.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ → clarify → component drop (on-device / cloud / hybrid with opt-in) → define test (accuracy threshold, battery, opt-in rate) → decision.
fields.Trap: Tech-first trap → choosing the more accurate cloud model despite the dominant privacy requirement.
fields.Defensible: P1 on-device default with opt-in cloud boost; P2 on-device only for children's albums; P3 cloud with explicit consent (accepts adoption loss).
fields.Reference trace: dominant requirement = privacy; accuracy 82% on a low-severity task is acceptable; battery 3% per 100 photos implies batch charging-time processing.
fields.Pump: "Let the single dominant user requirement break the tie."
fields.Retry seeds: privacy survey figure and accuracy gap.

title: A medical scribe with a hard safety floor

fields.Primer: Speed and cost are limited, errors in some fields are not / "1% error" means different things / Defend a configuration and how you will prove it.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM for a clinical note scribe. Constraint: at most 1% error on critical medications; budget $0.25 per visit; note ready within 8 seconds. Goal: choose the cheapest, fastest configuration that stays under the safety floor.
fields.Artifacts: R published studies show error rates depend on how they are counted: sentence-level hallucination 1.47% and omission 3.45% in one framework (S19); one audit found about one note in three with a verified failure (S20); omission is the most common type (S21). S configurations: A large model, full note: 0.6% medication error, 14 s, $0.42; B mid-size model + structured medication extraction + clinician confirmation: 0.9% before confirmation, 6 s, $0.18; C small model: 2.4%, 2 s, $0.05. S locked: E1(2) clinician confirmation: 85% of clinicians confirm; confirmation catches 90% of errors; E2(2) audit sample: 900 medication mentions; E3(2) severity: wrong dose S1; omitted allergy S1; wording S3.
fields.Run: Branch 1 define "error" (per entity, per sentence, per note) → Branch 2 configuration → Branch 3 validation plan → PROBE "How many tests do you need to claim under 1%?" → PUSHBACK if aggregate error is used → decision with hallucination budget by section.
fields.Trap: Average-metric trap → one aggregate error rate that hides critical medications.
fields.Defensible: P1 configuration B with mandatory confirmation for medications and allergies; P2 A for medication sections only, B for narrative (accepts complexity); P3 C for draft with full human edit (accepts clinician workload).
fields.Reference trace: B net error = 0.9% × (1 − 0.85 × 0.90) = 0.9% × 0.235 = 0.21% (still 0.5% if only 50% confirm); A fails cost ($0.42 > $0.25) and latency (14 s > 8 s); C fails safety (2.4%). Rule of three: 0 errors in n trials supports an upper bound of about 3/n, so to support under 1% you need about 300 error-free medication mentions.
fields.Pump: "Define the error unit and population before you argue about the rate."

title: A support copilot with three goals fighting

fields.Primer: Cost, speed and quality sit in tension / Customer data must not leak / Defend a routing design.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM for a support copilot that drafts replies. Goals: cost under $0.30 per ticket, reply drafts within 4 seconds (p95), and CSAT not lower than today.
fields.Artifacts: S 60% simple tickets, 40% complex; S models: large $0.12 per ticket with p95 5.5 s; small $0.02 with p95 1.8 s; router $0.005, misroutes 8% of complex tickets to the small model; S locked: E1(2) PII appears in 22% of tickets; E2(2) refunds above $100 require human approval; E3(2) pilot: small-model drafts on complex tickets cut CSAT by 0.4; E4(1) streaming reply display makes 5.5 s feel faster.
fields.Run: Branch 1 routing design → Branch 2 guardrails → Branch 3 evaluation → PROBE "What happens to misrouted tickets?" → PUSHBACK if redaction is missing → decision.
fields.Trap: Tech-first trap → picking the biggest model for everything or the cheapest for everything.
fields.Defensible: P1 router plus PII redaction before the model plus human approval for refunds; P2 small model first with escalate-on-low-confidence (accepts latency); P3 large for all complex tickets with streaming (accepts cost).
fields.Reference trace: blended cost = 0.6 × 0.02 + 0.4 × 0.12 + 0.005 = $0.065 (well under $0.30); misroutes = 0.4 × 8% = 3.2% of tickets; budget is not binding, quality and privacy are.
fields.Pump: "Find which constraint actually binds before optimising the others."
fields.Retry seeds: share of complex tickets; misroute rate.

title: Search relevance with a 300 ms budget

fields.Primer: A smarter ranker is slower and costlier / Many queries repeat / Defend where the smart part runs.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM for an e-commerce search. Goal: improve relevance within p95 latency of 300 ms and sensible cost.
fields.Artifacts: S retrieval p95 120 ms; cross-encoder rerank of top 30 adds 90 ms and +4.1% NDCG at $0.08 per 1,000 queries; LLM rerank adds 900 ms and +6.3% NDCG at $2.10 per 1,000; S locked: E1(2) top 20% of queries produce 65% of traffic; E2(2) catalogue changes daily; E3(2) users abandon above 2 s; E4(1) A/B test capacity: 2 weeks.
fields.Run: Branch 1 option (cross-encoder / LLM / hybrid) → Branch 2 caching strategy → Branch 3 test plan → PROBE "How do you ship the LLM benefit without the latency?" → decision.
fields.Trap: Tech-first trap → LLM rerank on every query.
fields.Defensible: P1 precompute LLM reranks for head queries daily and use the cross-encoder online for the tail; P2 cross-encoder only (accepts smaller uplift); P3 LLM rerank asynchronously for tail with later refresh (accepts complexity).
fields.Reference trace: hybrid uplift = 0.65 × 6.3% + 0.35 × 4.1% = 5.53%; online latency 120 + 90 = 210 ms (< 300); online cost 0.35 × $0.08 = $0.028 per 1,000 plus offline batch.
fields.Pump: "Move expensive work off the request path when many requests repeat."

title: The assistant is inventing fees in one region

fields.Primer: A fix in one place can break another / Money statements are high-severity / Defend isolation vs rollback and a shutdown rule.
fields.Scenario and goal: PayPilot (fictional fintech assistant). Goal: stop wrong-fee statements without wrecking the rest of the product.
fields.Artifacts: S Region R: 6.2% of fee answers wrong (1,840 audited); elsewhere 0.4% (9,200 audited); 38 complaints per day; regulator notification threshold: material misstatement to 100 or more customers in 72 hours; S locked: E1(2) cause: Region R fee table updated yesterday; retrieval index stale; E2(2) larger model reduces Region R errors to 1.1% but adds 2.1 s p95 latency and 3.1× cost globally; E3(2) deterministic fee lookup (no model) for fee questions: 2 engineer-days; E4(2) rollback of the global version loses two new features and the fix for another bug; E5(2) 11% of Region R users who saw a wrong fee proceeded with a transfer; E6(2) monitoring: a judge model can grade fee answers on a rolling sample.
fields.Run: Branch 1 isolate/rollback/larger model → Branch 2 segment priority → PIVOT "The larger model deploy shows latency spikes in all regions and support queues double" → PROBE "Where is the auto-shutdown threshold and why?" → PROBE "Who do you notify, and when?" → PUSHBACK on a global fix for a local fault → decision with thresholds.
fields.Trap: Fix-forward cascade trap → a global model swap for a regional data fault.
fields.Defensible: P1 feature-flag Region R, route fee questions to deterministic lookup globally, fix the index; P2 roll back the global version (accepts feature loss); P3 isolate and keep the larger model only for Region R (accepts cost there).
fields.Reference trace: fault is data staleness; deterministic lookup removes the model from the risky path; auto-shutdown: if wrong-fee rate ≥ 1.5% over a rolling 200-answer audit sample in any region (about 4× the 0.4% baseline and below the point where the notification threshold is reached), switch that region to deterministic lookup and page on-call; notification clock: 72 hours.
fields.Pump: "Fix the layer where the fault lives; keep the blast radius equal to the damage radius."

title: An agent that can spend money

fields.Primer: An assistant can act, not only answer / Some actions can be undone, some cannot / Defend which actions need a human.
fields.Scenario and goal: BookBuddy (fictional travel agent). Goal: set the autonomy policy for an agent that can search, hold, message vendors and purchase.
fields.Artifacts: S 50,000 purchases attempted per day; 12% of sessions touch untrusted web pages; red-team: 3 of 200 injected pages (1.5%) triggered an unauthorised action; S locked: E1(2) action reversibility: search and hold (reversible, 15-minute hold); purchase under $200 (refundable 24 h); purchase over $200 (non-refundable for 40% of airline tickets); E2(2) average ticket $320; 30% of unauthorised actions are purchases; E3(2) confirmation steps reduce conversion by 6% each; E4(2) allow-listed domains reduce injection exposure by 80%; E5(2) cost of a human confirmation: $0.04.
fields.Run: Branch 1 autonomy tiers → Branch 2 mitigations → PIVOT "A new attack bypasses the allow-list in a test" → PROBE "Which action never runs without a human?" → PROBE "What is your acceptable loss per day?" → decision with a monitoring rule.
fields.Trap: Tech-first trap → maximising autonomy because the demo is impressive.
fields.Defensible: P1 tiers by reversibility and value: free autonomy for search and hold, confirmation for non-refundable or over $50, plus allow-lists and an action log; P2 confirm every purchase (accepts conversion loss); P3 limit to fares with free cancellation (accepts a smaller catalogue).
fields.Reference trace: unmitigated unauthorised actions per day = 50,000 × 12% × 1.5% = 90; purchases 27; expected exposure = 27 × $320 × 40% non-refundable = about $3,456 per day; allow-lists cut exposure by 80%; confirmation on non-refundable purchases removes most of the remainder.
fields.Pump: "Tie each action's autonomy to how reversible it is and how much it can cost."

title: Monday 8 a.m.: 10,000 clinicians at once

fields.Primer: The system is built for fewer users than will arrive / Not every part of a note is equally risky / Defend what you degrade and what you protect.
fields.Scenario and goal: The medical scribe from AIT-M-1 launches to a health network. Capacity at full quality: 6,500 concurrent sessions; expected peak 10,000. Goal: decide the degrade policy.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(2) note sections: medications and allergies (S1), assessment and plan (S2), narrative history (S2/S3), billing suggestions (advisory); E2(2) smaller model handles narrative with 3% acceptable edit rate; E3(2) async note finalisation allowed within 10 minutes; E4(2) queueing: wait over 90 s makes clinicians abandon; E5(2) retrieval of clinic templates vs fine-tune for tone; E6(2) hallucination budget workshop outcomes from clinicians.
fields.Run: Branch 1 degrade vs queue vs outage → Branch 2 hallucination budget by section → PIVOT "The template retrieval service fails at 8:10" → PROBE "Retrieval or fine-tuning for clinic style?" → PROBE "What is your kill-switch?" → decision with thresholds.
fields.Trap: Tech-first trap / fix-forward cascade → buying capacity or a bigger model instead of protecting what matters.
fields.Defensible: P1 keep full quality for S1 sections, route narrative to a smaller model, finalise asynchronously; P2 queue with an honest wait time for non-urgent clinics (accepts abandonment); P3 staged rollout by clinic (accepts delay).
fields.Reference trace: demand/capacity = 10,000 ÷ 6,500 = 1.54×; moving narrative (about 60% of load, assumed) to a model costing a third as much brings load under capacity; template style by retrieval because templates change quarterly; kill-switch: medication-section error rate in sampled audits above the budget triggers deterministic form entry.
fields.Pump: "Degrade the part with the lowest severity first, and say so out loud."

title: You disagreed with a designer about feature placement

fields.Primer: Two good ideas, one screen / The disagreement is about users, not people / Be ready to say exactly what you did and what you learned.
fields.Scene: A design review. The designer wants the "Share" button moved into a menu. You believe it will reduce use. Choices: A) ask to look at usage data together first; B) propose a quick test of both placements; C) go with the designer and revisit later.
fields.Story prompt: "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a designer or an engineer about how something should work."
fields.Probes by scene choice: A → "What data did you look at and what did it say?"; B → "How did you decide the test was fair?"; C → "What made you let it go, and what happened?" Standard: "What did you say first?" "What did you learn about working with them?"
fields.Signals: one clear disagreement; the user's own moves; evidence used; a result; a learning applied later.
fields.Trap: We-washing → every action stated as "we".
fields.Defensible stories: resolved by data; by a test; by a compromise; by deferring with a defined review date.
fields.Reference trace (shape, not a script): situation with stakes (launch in 3 weeks) → "I asked for the click data on Share by placement" → "I proposed a 5% test" → result: share rate 7.8% vs 6.1% → "I now ask for the decision criterion before debating options".
fields.Pump: "Describe the first sentence you said to the designer, word for word."
fields.Retry: same prompt with a different scene (the disagreement is with an engineer).

title: You learned something fast to ship something

fields.Primer: A deadline with a knowledge gap / Show how you closed the gap / Say what you did, not what the team did.
fields.Scene: Monday morning: a launch depends on a payments rule you do not understand. Choices: A) book time with the payments lead; B) read the policy and draft a summary; C) ask your manager to reassign.
fields.Story prompt: "Tell me about a time you had to learn something quickly to deliver."
fields.Probes: "What did you do in the first 24 hours?" "How did you know you understood it?" "Who did you check with?" "What would you do differently?"
fields.Signals: concrete learning actions; validation of understanding; delivery outcome; reuse of the learning.
fields.Trap: We-washing.
fields.Defensible stories: mentor-led learning; self-study with expert review; scoping down to what was learnable.
fields.Reference trace: "I listed what I did not know (3 items) → asked the payments lead for 30 minutes → wrote a one-page summary and had them correct it → launched on time; I now keep a 'rules I rely on' page."
fields.Pump: "Name the single question that unblocked you and who answered it."
fields.Retry: the knowledge gap is technical rather than regulatory.

title: Customer feedback changed your decision

fields.Primer: You had a plan; a customer disagreed / Evidence beats opinion / Show what you did with the feedback.
fields.Scene: A customer call reveals that your feature is confusing. Choices: A) ask to see them use it; B) check usage data for the same pattern; C) note it and move on.
fields.Story prompt: "Tell me about a time customer feedback changed what you were going to do."
fields.Probes: "How many customers, and how did you know it was not one voice?" "What did you change?" "What was the result?"
fields.Signals: validation beyond a single anecdote; a decision change; a measured result.
fields.Trap: We-washing / generic story.
fields.Defensible stories: data-confirmed change; test-then-change; deciding not to change after validation (also valid).
fields.Reference trace: "Three calls and a usage check showed 40% abandoned at step 2; I proposed removing the step; completion went from 52% to 61%; I now pair every anecdote with a count."
fields.Pump: "State how you separated one loud customer from a pattern."
fields.Retry: feedback comes from an internal sales team.

title: Stability versus the hard date

fields.Primer: Two legitimate goals collide / No outcome satisfies both fully / Be honest about what each side gave up.
fields.Scene: Release meeting: engineering wants two more weeks for stability; the business has a promised date. Choices: A) ship on time with a reduced scope; B) delay and renegotiate; C) ship on time and plan a hotfix window.
fields.Story prompt: "Tell me about a time you had to balance engineering's need for stability with a business deadline."
fields.Probes: "What exactly did you trade away?" "How did each side react?" "What would you have done with one more week?" "Who was slightly unhappy and why?"
fields.Signals: trade-off named; explicit cost; imperfect outcome accepted; communication of the decision; learning.
fields.Trap: Tidy resolution → "everyone was happy".
fields.Defensible stories: scope cut; staged rollout; delayed date with a negotiated commitment; hotfix plan.
fields.Reference trace: "Defined the must-have path → cut 2 of 5 features → agreed a feature-flagged rollout to 10% → date kept; engineering was unhappy about the flag overhead; retrospective shortened the next release checklist."
fields.Pump: "Say what each side lost, in one sentence each."
fields.Retry: the conflict is between design quality and a date.

title: Saying no to a senior stakeholder's idea

fields.Primer: A senior person wants something you think is wrong for the product / Tone and evidence both matter / Show what you did, not just what you believed.
fields.Scene: An executive asks you to add a feature to the roadmap this quarter. Choices: A) ask what outcome they want and offer options; B) present data against it; C) agree and quietly deprioritise.
fields.Story prompt: "Tell me about a time you pushed back on a senior stakeholder."
fields.Probes: "What did you say?" "What did they do?" "What did the relationship look like afterwards?" "What did it cost you?"
fields.Signals: respectful challenge; alternative offered; evidence; commit after decision; honest cost.
fields.Trap: Tidy resolution (or hero narrative: "I proved them wrong").
fields.Defensible stories: reframing to outcomes; testing a small version; escalating with a trade-off table.
fields.Reference trace: "Asked for the outcome behind the request → showed that 3 other items moved the same metric more → proposed a smaller pilot → agreed; later results were mixed; I now bring a trade-off table to such conversations."
fields.Pump: "Quote the sentence where you stated your concern."

title: A dependency slipped and two teams wanted different things

fields.Primer: You depend on a team you do not manage / Both teams have good reasons / Show influence without authority.
fields.Scene: Another team's API will be late. Your team wants to wait; theirs wants to change the contract. Choices: A) escalate; B) propose an interim solution; C) ask both for a shared goal meeting.
fields.Story prompt: "Tell me about a time you had to influence a team you did not manage."
fields.Probes: "What did you offer them?" "What did you give up?" "How did you know they agreed?"
fields.Signals: understanding the other team's constraint; a concrete proposal; follow-through; an imperfect compromise.
fields.Trap: Tidy resolution.
fields.Defensible stories: interim shim; contract change with versioning; scope staging.
fields.Reference trace: "Mapped both teams' deadlines → proposed a versioned contract with a two-week shim → got sign-off in writing → shipped two weeks late; documented a dependency checklist."
fields.Pump: "Say what the other team needed that you had not known."

title: The project is failing in front of the board

fields.Primer: A high-stakes room and bad news / You own the outcome whatever the cause / Show what you said, what you chose and what you recorded.
fields.Scene: 10 p.m. before a board review: a flagship project is three months late and over budget. Choices: A) present the truth with a recovery plan; B) ask for a delay to the meeting; C) present a rosy status and fix it quietly.
fields.Story prompt: "Tell me about a time a project you led was failing and you had to tell leadership."
fields.Probes: "What exactly did you tell them?" "What option did you reject, and why?" "What did it cost you personally?" "What did you document?"
fields.Signals: ownership; trade-off communicated; options presented; a recovery or an honest stop; a written learning.
fields.Trap: Hero/blame narrative → blaming others or a flawless rescue.
fields.Defensible stories: restructured scope; stopped the project; secured a smaller deliverable; handed over with a post-mortem.
fields.Reference trace: "I wrote the three options with costs → told leadership which I recommended and why → cut scope by 40% → delivered a smaller version; I wrote a post-mortem naming my own estimation mistake."
fields.Pump: "Describe the moment you realised it was drifting, and the first thing you told the team."
fields.Retry: the project failed rather than recovered.

title: An incident harmed users and you owned the response

fields.Primer: Something you shipped hurt people / Speed and honesty compete / Show your decisions in the first hour.
fields.Scene: A release exposes some users' data in a feed. Choices: A) disable the feature at once and notify; B) investigate first, then decide; C) patch silently.
fields.Story prompt: "Tell me about a time your product caused harm or a serious incident and what you did."
fields.Probes: "What did you decide in the first hour?" "Who did you tell and when?" "What did you stop doing afterwards?" "How did you know it was fixed?"
fields.Signals: rapid containment; honest communication; ownership; measured recovery; systemic fix.
fields.Trap: Hero/blame narrative or a sanitised story.
fields.Defensible stories: disclose first; contain first then disclose within a defined window (both can be justified with the trade-off).
fields.Reference trace: "I pulled the feature within 20 minutes → drafted the notice with legal → told affected users within 24 hours → added a pre-release privacy check; 0 repeat incidents in two quarters."
fields.Pump: "State the first action and the time it took."
fields.Retry: the incident was a pricing mistake rather than a privacy one.

title: You found your own number was wrong after presenting it

fields.Primer: A mistake of yours is already in the room / Admitting it early costs less than late / Show what you did and what you changed.
fields.Scene: Two days after a leadership review you discover a metric you presented was overstated. Choices: A) tell leadership now with the corrected number; B) wait for the next review; C) correct it quietly in the dashboard.
fields.Story prompt: "Tell me about a time you made a significant mistake in your work and what you did about it."
fields.Probes: "Who did you tell first?" "What was the effect of the correction?" "What changed in how you work?" "What did you do about trust?"
fields.Signals: ownership; speed; transparency; consequences accepted; process change.
fields.Trap: Polished lie → a trivial mistake presented as a failure, or a perfect recovery.
fields.Defensible stories: immediate disclosure; disclosure after verifying (with a short window); correction with a visible log.
fields.Reference trace: "I verified the error in 2 hours → emailed my lead and the exec with the corrected figure and cause → the decision was delayed a week; I added a reconciliation check to the dashboard."
fields.Pump: "Describe the sentence you used to disclose the mistake."
fields.Retry: the mistake belonged to a teammate and you owned the communication.

title: Finding items in a huge grocery store

fields.Primer: Shoppers lose time in a big store / One friction, one group / Defend one solution and one measurable result.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM at a grocery chain (fictional "FreshMart"). Goal: reduce the time shoppers spend searching for an item.
fields.Artifacts: S store 38,000 sq ft; 28,000 items; observed average time to find an unfamiliar item 6.5 minutes (50 shoppers); S locked: E1(1) shopper types: weekly stock-up 55%, quick trip 30%, senior 15%; E2(1) quotes: "I walk past it twice"; "staff are always busy"; E3(2) 22% of shoppers give up on an item per trip; E4(2) staff on the floor: 1 per 6,000 sq ft; E5(2) 70% of shoppers have the store app installed.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ (friction vs symptom; what a good metric looks like; why one group first) → scope persona (weekly stock-up shopper) → validate friction → idea board (in-aisle location markers / app item locator / staff paging / loyalty points / AR navigation) → kill one → metric (average time to find an item) and a test → claim.
fields.Trap: Solution-first trap → jumping to AR navigation before validating the friction.
fields.Defensible: P1 app item locator plus aisle markers (accepts app dependency); P2 shelf labels and staff paging (accepts staff load); P3 a simple printed map at entrances for seniors.
fields.Reference trace: persona = stock-up shopper; friction = unfamiliar locations plus no help; metric: median time to find an item (6.5 → under 4 minutes) in test stores vs control; guardrail: basket size does not fall.
fields.Pump: "State the friction as something you could observe on a camera."

title: Parents keep returning kids' clothes

fields.Primer: Returns are high for one category / The reason is more specific than "fit" / Defend a feature and the number that proves it.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM at an online kids' apparel shop. Return rate is 31%. Goal: cut returns without raising prices.
fields.Artifacts: S return reasons: wrong size 46%, quality 18%, changed mind 20%, other 16%; S locked: E1(1) parents buy one size up 57% of the time; E2(1) growth between ordering and wearing: 6 weeks average; E3(2) size charts differ across brands; E4(2) returns cost $9 each; E5(2) 62% shop on mobile.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ → scope persona (first-time parent of a toddler / parent of a 6–10 year old / gift buyer) → validate → ideas (size recommender using birthdate and height / free returns / reviews with child height / chat assistant / loyalty points) → kill one → metric (size-related return rate) → claim.
fields.Trap: Solution-first trap → building a chatbot.
fields.Defensible: P1 size recommender by age and height with brand mapping; P2 "size up" prompts and growth-aware suggestions; P3 reviews that show child height.
fields.Reference trace: size reasons are 46% of 31% = 14.3% of orders; halving gives −7.1 points; test: holdout by region; guardrail: conversion does not fall.
fields.Pump: "Tie the metric to the exact return reason you target."

title: New gym members stop after three weeks

fields.Primer: Motivation fades when the next step is unclear / A common reason hides behind "lack of time" / Defend a feature and its proof.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM for a fitness app. Goal: improve four-week retention of new users.
fields.Artifacts: S four-week retention 24%; S locked: E1(1) lapsed users survey: "didn't know what to do" 52%, time 21%, cost 12%, injury 8%, other 7%; E2(1) users with a plan: retention 41%; E3(2) 70% of lapsed users stopped on a day with no scheduled workout; E4(2) average session 28 minutes; E5(2) coach messages: 4% open.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ → persona (beginner / returning athlete / casual walker) → validate → ideas (next-workout suggestion / streak badges / social challenges / coach chat / AI plans) → kill → metric → claim.
fields.Trap: Solution-first trap → gamification before the friction.
fields.Defensible: P1 a clear next-workout card with 3 options; P2 a short onboarding plan; P3 a coach prompt only when the user is stuck.
fields.Reference trace: 52% cite not knowing what to do; plan users retain 41% vs 24% (selection bias noted); metric: four-week retention of users who start a plan; guardrail: completion not just starts.
fields.Pump: "Choose the idea that attacks the largest named reason, then check the reason is real."

title: A first IKEA visit for a new homeowner

fields.Primer: A big, maze-like store intimidates first-time buyers / The goal is feeling capable, not feature use / Defend how you will know anxiety dropped.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM at a home-furnishing retailer (fictional "NestHouse"). Goal: make the first visit less intimidating for new homeowners.
fields.Artifacts: S three floors, one-way path; S locked: E1(2) 8 interviews: "I don't know where to start"; "I can't picture it at home"; "I forgot the measurements"; E2(2) 38% leave without buying the main item; E3(2) staff cannot help with room planning; E4(2) app has a floor plan but 9% use it; E5(2) returns of bulky items 14%; E6(2) 60% of visitors arrive with an unplanned list.
fields.Run: Branch 1 define friction (wayfinding / planning / commitment anxiety) → Branch 2 persona → idea board (pre-visit room planner / guided route by list / "starter kit" bundles / in-store planning kiosks / AI chat) → kill one → metric (a verified measure of reduced anxiety: 3-question confidence pulse plus list completion) → PROBE "How would you know the guide is not just another thing to look at?" → claim.
fields.Trap: Assumed user trap → assuming wayfinding is the problem without validating.
