fields.Defensible: P1 pre-visit planner plus a guided route; P2 starter bundles for first-time buyers (accepts less choice); P3 in-store planning kiosks with staff (accepts cost).
fields.Reference trace: friction = not knowing where to start and forgetting measurements; metric: confidence pulse +1 point (5-point scale) and list completion 60% → 80%; test: A/B by visit week; guardrail: time in store.
fields.Pump: "Say how you would measure the feeling, not just the clicks."

title: First-time riders and the intercity bus

fields.Primer: People avoid what feels unreliable / The anxiety is about the unknown at the stop / Defend a solution and the proof it helps.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM for a bus booking app (fictional "SawariGo") on a long-distance route. Goal: increase repeat bookings among first-time riders.
fields.Artifacts: S first-time riders 62% of bookings; repeat rate 18%; S locked: E1(2) interviews: "I did not know where the bus stops"; "no live location"; "I paid cash because I did not trust the app"; E2(2) 27% of first-time riders contact support on departure day; E3(1) 35% travel with luggage and children; E4(2) mobile network gaps on the route; E5(2) refunds take 7 days.
fields.Run: Branch 1 define friction → persona (solo first-timer / family / elderly) → ideas (boarding-point photo and pin / live location with offline fallback / SMS reminder with driver number / digital refunds in 24 hours / rewards points) → kill one → metric (repeat booking within 60 days and departure-day contact rate) → claim.
fields.Trap: Assumed user trap → designing for always-on connectivity.
fields.Defensible: P1 boarding-point guide with offline fallback; P2 SMS driver contact; P3 faster refunds.
fields.Reference trace: connectivity gaps imply offline-first design; metric pair: contact rate −30%, repeat rate 18% → 24%.
fields.Pump: "Test your solution against the worst phone and the worst signal."

title: A telehealth app for adults over 45

fields.Primer: A first video visit fails often / The reason may be confidence, not technology / Defend how you will know it helps.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM for a telehealth app. 34% of first appointments fail to connect. Goal: raise first-visit completion among adults 45+.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(2) failures: permissions/camera 41%, wrong link or time 23%, audio problems 18%, gave up waiting 18%; E2(2) 64% use a phone browser; E3(2) older users call support 3× more often; E4(2) clinician no-show wait: 10 minutes; E5(2) caregiver helps in 20% of visits.
fields.Run: Branch 1 friction → persona → ideas (pre-visit tech check / one-tap join link with SMS / caregiver invite / phone-call fallback / video tutorial) → kill one → metric (first-visit completion; confidence pulse) → PROBE "What does a clinician lose with your design?" → claim.
fields.Trap: Assumed user trap → assuming every user installs an app.
fields.Defensible: P1 one-tap SMS link plus pre-visit check; P2 phone fallback; P3 caregiver invite.
fields.Reference trace: permissions 41% + wrong link 23% = 64% addressable by the pre-visit check and SMS link; target completion 66% → 80%.
fields.Pump: "Match each idea to the share of failures it actually removes."

title: How older residents of Tokyo move through the transit system

fields.Primer: A very large group, a very complex system / "Elderly" is not one user / Defend who you serve, what you build, and how you measure independence.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM at a transit-tech company (fictional). Goal: define an audience, a problem and a product vision that improves older residents' independence.
fields.Artifacts: R Japan's 65+ share is 29.4% of the population (2025 census, S18); the ministry estimates 29.6% or about 36.2 million people. S locked: E1(2) interviews: station complexity; fear of mistakes at gates; elevator locations hard to find; transfers under time pressure; E2(2) segment sizes: active 65–74 (12.5% of the population) vs 75+ (16.8%); E3(2) smartphone use differs sharply by age; E4(2) station staff availability; E5(2) women outnumber men in the 65+ group.
fields.Run: Branch 1 define audience (choose or define) → Branch 2 problem framing → idea board → PROBE "Why this group first?" → KILL-YOUR-DARLING → PIVOT "Operator allows one change only" → metric of independence (trips made without assistance; avoided trips; confidence) → claim.
fields.Trap: Laundry-list trap → listing ten features for "the elderly".
fields.Defensible: P1 audience 75+ living alone, single-trip confidence aid; P2 audience 65–74 active commuters, transfer planning; P3 caregiver-linked assistance (accepts a smaller user base).
fields.Reference trace: independence measures: share of trips taken without help; trips avoided because of fear; self-reported confidence; each is verifiable by a diary panel.
fields.Pump: "Narrow the audience until a single sentence describes their worst moment."

title: Designing for first-time flyers

fields.Primer: A wide-open space with many easy ideas / A good product feels coherent / Defend what you cut as much as what you build.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM at an airline or airport app (fictional). Goal: design a travel experience for first-time flyers.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(2) 3 personas: nervous solo adult, family with kids, older traveller visiting relatives; E2(2) biggest frictions by persona: documents and airport procedures, boarding and gate changes, what to expect at security; E3(2) first-timers' no-show rate 3× higher; E4(2) average airport dwell 2.4 hours; E5(2) app adoption 28%; E6(2) staff capacity: limited.
fields.Run: Branch 1 audience → Branch 2 friction validation → idea board (checklist, step-by-step journey, live gate guide, buddy chat, rewards, AI travel assistant, kiosk, SMS nudges) → KILL → PROBE "What would you not build, and for whom?" → metric (on-time arrival at gate; confidence pulse; support contacts) → claim.
fields.Trap: Feature-factory trap → a laundry list instead of a coherent product.
fields.Defensible: P1 a single "what happens next" journey card with notifications; P2 a staff-assisted first-timer lane (accepts staff cost); P3 SMS-first guidance (accepts less rich).
fields.Reference trace: persona = nervous solo adult; friction = fear of the unknown at security and gates; core: next-step card + proactive nudges; killed: rewards and chat.
fields.Pump: "Say what unites your features; if nothing does, cut until something does."

title: Fair price information for a farmers' cooperative

fields.Primer: Information gaps hurt one side of a market / The users have limited phones and time / Defend who benefits first and how you will know.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM at an agri-tech start-up in Nepal (fictional). Goal: design a product that helps smallholder farmers in a cooperative get fairer prices, and measure impact on their income.
fields.Artifacts: S cooperative of 600 farmers; 41% have feature phones only; S farm-gate prices are on average 28% below the wholesale market price (assumed illustrative); S locked: E1(2) interviews: farmers learn prices by word of mouth; middlemen offer the same price to all; E2(2) transport costs: a shared truck costs NPR 9,000 per trip; E3(2) literacy: 35% prefer voice; E4(2) mobile coverage: patchy in two villages; E5(2) the cooperative has a manager who negotiates; E6(2) one bad harvest erodes trust in any new tool.
fields.Run: Branch 1 define the user (farmer / cooperative manager / both) → Branch 2 friction → ideas (SMS price alerts / voice IVR / shared transport booking / grading and quality certificates / app marketplace) → KILL → PROBE "What if only the middleman uses it?" → metric of income (price realised vs wholesale benchmark; share of produce sold above the farm-gate average) → claim.
fields.Trap: Laundry-list trap / assumed user trap → an app marketplace for farmers without smartphones.
fields.Defensible: P1 SMS/voice price alerts for the cooperative plus manager dashboard; P2 shared transport booking to cut costs; P3 grading to earn a premium (accepts slower impact).
fields.Reference trace: audience = cooperative manager plus farmers via voice/SMS; metric = realised price vs benchmark over a season; guardrail = no increase in farmer costs.
fields.Pump: "Choose the channel your least-connected user actually uses."
fields.Retry seeds: share with feature phones and price gap.

title: Daily actives fell 10% in three weeks

fields.Primer: A headline metric is down / Not every user group moved / Defend the metric you track to know recovery and the next step.
fields.Scenario and goal: FitPulse (fictional fitness app). DAU 480,000 → 432,000 in three weeks. Goal: pick the success metric, a guardrail and one measurable next step.
fields.Artifacts: S dashboard; locked: E1(1) DAU by cohort: core users 365,000 → 365,000 (flat); January-challenge cohort 115,000 → 67,000; E2(1) same period last year: −8% with the same cohort pattern; E3(1) platform and region: flat (red herring); E4(2) lapsed challenge users (not active 14+ days): 48,000; E5(2) campaign history: opt-out rate 1.8% per re-engagement campaign.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ (DAU vs retention; cohort effects; what a guardrail is) → clarify → evidence → Metric Tree (primary + guardrail) → experiment card → claim.
fields.Trap: Vanity recovery → restoring the DAU number with broad push notifications.
fields.Defensible: P1 target the 48,000 lapsed challenge users with a restart plan and a 10% holdout; P2 do nothing and track core-user retention (accepts the seasonal decline); P3 improve onboarding for the next cohort (accepts delay).
fields.Reference trace: decline is entirely the challenge cohort (115k → 67k = −48k); primary metric: 14-day reactivation rate of lapsed challenge users; guardrails: notification opt-out ≤ 2.5% and completed workouts per reactivated user; success: +4,800 reactivated (10%) vs holdout.
fields.Pump: "Break the headline into groups before choosing what to recover."

title: How to prove "Save for later" works

fields.Primer: A new feature needs a success metric before launch / Counting saves is easy and weak / Defend a metric, a guardrail and a test.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM for a shopping app launching "Save for later". Goal: define success and a test.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(1) pilot: 3.1 saves per user per week; E2(1) 6% of saved items are purchased within 14 days; E3(2) baseline checkout conversion of eligible users: 3.0%; eligible users 8,000 per day; E4(2) risk: users save instead of buying; E5(2) return rate baseline 12%.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ → clarify → evidence → Metric Tree → experiment card (arms, sample, duration) → claim.
fields.Trap: Vanity recovery (vanity metric) → "number of saves" as the primary metric.
fields.Defensible: P1 primary: purchases from saved items within 14 days per exposed user; guardrail: overall checkout conversion; P2 primary: 28-day revenue per eligible user (accepts a longer wait).
fields.Reference trace: detect +0.3 points on a 3.0% base: n ≈ 15.7 × 0.03 × 0.97 ÷ 0.003² = 50,763 per arm; 4,000 users/day/arm → 12.7 days → run 14 days; guardrail: conversion not down more than 0.1 point.
fields.Pump: "Choose the metric that would still look good if saves were only a place to forget things."

title: More orders: how will you know it is healthy?

fields.Primer: A growth number can rise for the wrong reason / The growth is one part of the picture / Defend the metric and the guardrail.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM at a food-delivery app. Goal: increase orders per user.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(1) total orders +9% month on month; active users +9% (promo acquisition); orders per active user 2.1 (flat); E2(1) cancellation rate 6.0% → 7.5% at peak hours; E3(2) late deliveries 11%; E4(2) reorder behavior: 38% of orders are repeat of a past order; E5(2) test capacity: 3 weeks.
fields.Run: RF 3 MCQ → clarify → evidence → Metric Tree → experiment card → claim.
fields.Trap: Vanity recovery → celebrating total orders.
fields.Defensible: P1 a one-tap reorder test with primary orders per active user per week and guardrails on lateness and cancellations; P2 a free-delivery threshold test (accepts margin cost).
fields.Reference trace: total orders rose because of more users, not more orders per user; target +0.15 orders per user per week; stop rule: late deliveries above 12% or cancellations above 6.5%.
fields.Pump: "Divide a total by the right population before you celebrate."

title: Notifications lift daily actives and uninstalls

fields.Primer: A growth metric and a health metric disagree / Different users react differently / Defend the balance and the test.
fields.Scenario and goal: PingPal (fictional social app). A new notification strategy raised DAU 2.00M → 2.16M (+8%); weekly uninstalls rose 10,000 → 13,840. Goal: find the sweet spot between growth and annoyance.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(1) DAU by segment: light users 0.50M → 0.58M (+16%); heavy users 1.50M → 1.58M (+5%); E2(2) weekly uninstall rate: light 0.50% → 1.10% (base 800k); heavy 0.50% → 0.42% (base 1.2M); E3(1) notifications per day: light 2.1 → 4.6; heavy 2.1 → 2.4; E4(2) notification disable rate: light 3% → 9%; E5(2) 28-day retention for new users: −2.5 points; E6(1) crash and releases: flat (red herring).
fields.Run: Branch 1 segment → Branch 2 choose a primary retention metric and guardrail → experiment card (arms: 2.1, 3, 4.6 per day for light users) → PROBE "Who actually drives the uninstalls?" → PUSHBACK if the aggregate DAU is the success metric → claim.
fields.Trap: Primary-metric tunnel → optimising DAU.
fields.Defensible: P1 cap light-user notification frequency at about 3 per day with adaptive relevance; P2 keep volume for heavy users only; P3 roll back and test relevance not frequency.
fields.Reference trace: uninstalls: light 800,000 × 1.10% = 8,800; heavy 1.2M × 0.42% = 5,040 → 13,840 (0.69% of 2.0M); the increase is from light users who receive 4.6 notifications a day.
fields.Pump: "Find which segment drives the guardrail breach before changing the lever."

title: Raise checkout conversion by 5%

fields.Primer: A numeric target and a tempting shortcut / Customers notice hidden costs / Defend how you hit the goal without hurting trust.
fields.Scenario and goal: BuyLane (fictional retailer). Goal: raise checkout conversion from 3.00% to 3.15% (+5%).
fields.Artifacts: R Baymard reports about 70% average cart abandonment and extra costs as the leading reason (reported 39% to 48% depending on the survey year) (S17); S locked: E1(1) funnel by device: mobile abandons 31% at the payment step; E2(1) by region: Region B abandons 41% after seeing shipping fees; E3(2) experiment results: Variant H (hide shipping until the last step): conversion +6.2%, 30-day repeat purchase −9%, "unexpected fee" tickets +45%, chargebacks +0.3 points; Variant S (show a shipping estimate in the cart plus free-shipping progress): conversion +4.1%, repeat flat, tickets −8%; Variant G (guest checkout): +3.4%; E4(2) support cost per ticket $4.20; E5(2) average order value $62.
fields.Run: Branch 1 find the failure point (cut by device and region) → Branch 2 pick variants → PROBE "Variant H beats your goal; why not ship it?" → PUSHBACK if no guardrail is named → experiment card with decision rule → claim.
fields.Trap: Metric tunnel → shipping Variant H.
fields.Defensible: P1 Variant S plus G combined, test with guardrails on repeat purchase and tickets; P2 Variant S only; P3 Variant H with a long holdout and kill rule (accepts risk).
fields.Reference trace: H hits the goal (+6.2%) but erodes trust (repeat −9%); S +4.1% and G +3.4% together plausibly exceed +5% without harming repeat; guardrails: repeat purchase, fee tickets, chargebacks.
fields.Pump: "Name a metric that would reveal the damage your fix could cause."

title: A referral program with suspicious signups

fields.Primer: Signups rose but quality is unclear / Rewards change behavior / Defend what you reward and how you test it.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM for a finance app's referral program. Goal: grow activated users at a sustainable cost.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(1) referral signups 40,000 per month at $4 each ($160,000); E2(1) 7-day activation: referred 18% vs organic 41%; E3(2) self-referral and duplicate-device rate 14%; E4(2) pilot of "pay on activation $12": signups 28,000; activation 35%; E5(2) support cost per fraud case $18; E6(2) test capacity: 4 weeks.
fields.Run: Branch 1 define the primary metric (signups / activated users / revenue) → Branch 2 guardrails → experiment card (control vs pay-on-activation; holdout) → PROBE "How do you separate fraud from real referrals?" → claim.
fields.Trap: Metric tunnel → rewarding signups.
fields.Defensible: P1 pay on activation with fraud checks; P2 tiered reward (small at signup, larger at activation); P3 cap rewards per user.
fields.Reference trace: current cost per activated user = $160,000 ÷ (40,000 × 18% = 7,200) = $22.2; pilot: 28,000 × 35% = 9,800 activated; 9,800 × $12 = $117,600 → $12.0 per activated user.
fields.Pump: "Reward the behavior you want to see after the signup."

title: Watch time is at a record, but is it healthy?

fields.Primer: The tracked metric looks perfect / The quiet metric may be failing / Defend a test that can show it.
fields.Scenario and goal: StreamNest (fictional) watch time is at an all-time high (+9% year on year). Goal: decide whether to test an algorithm that promotes content diversity.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(1) 90-day retention flat; monthly churn 2.4% → 2.7%; E2(2) diversity index (distinct genres per user per month) 4.1 → 3.2; top 5% of titles' share of viewing 31% → 44%; E3(2) at equal watch time, users with ≤2 genres churn 3.4% vs 1.9% for 5+ genres (confounding warning); E4(2) exit survey: "nothing new to watch" up 11 points; E5(2) experiment capacity: one test with a 5% holdout for 12 weeks; E6(2) leadership target: watch time must not fall more than 3%.
fields.Run: Branch 1 test whether the tracked metric predicts the outcome → Branch 2 design (primary: 90-day retention and churn; guardrail: watch time ≥ −3%) → PIVOT "Quarter-end: leadership wants the watch-time record kept" → PROBE "Why would more diversity be better?" → PROBE "How long do you run it?" → PUSHBACK on causal claims from E3 → claim with stop rules.
fields.Trap: Silent-metric blindness → optimising watch time only.
fields.Defensible: P1 12-week holdout with retention as primary and watch time as guardrail; P2 a smaller diversity nudge first (accepts slower learning); P3 survey-first to verify demand (accepts weaker evidence).
fields.Reference trace: E3 is correlational (heavy single-genre viewers may differ); the test breaks the confound by randomising; need a retention effect size: with churn ~2.4% a difference of 0.3 points over 12 weeks; stop rule if watch time falls more than 3%.
fields.Pump: "Ask whether the metric you celebrate predicts the outcome you need."

title: Active users are up 22%; is anyone new actually there?

fields.Primer: AI products attract automated usage / Activity is not the same as people / Defend what counts as an active user.
fields.Scenario and goal: ChatNook (fictional AI assistant). Weekly active users 1.00M → 1.22M; events +61%. Goal: decide the right metric and a safe fix.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(2) a labelled sample of 2,000 sessions: automated traffic share of new events 52%; E2(2) automation signals: fixed-interval requests, API-key traffic, no UI events; E3(2) retention of human users flat; revenue per active user −9%; E4(2) some automation is legitimate (paying API customers, 8% of revenue); E5(2) classifier precision 0.92 and recall 0.81 on the sample; E6(2) new events 24.4M: of which 52% automated = 12.7M; E7(2) leadership: a board slide uses WAU.
fields.Run: Branch 1 validate the metric → Branch 2 redefine (human WAU; automation tracked separately) → PIVOT "A big customer's automation was misclassified as human and complains" → PROBE "How do you treat legitimate automation?" → PROBE "What do you tell the board?" → experiment/validation card → claim.
fields.Trap: Silent-metric blindness → celebrating raw WAU.
fields.Defensible: P1 report human WAU and automated usage separately; improve the classifier with a labelled audit; P2 define "verified human sessions" with a UI-event requirement (accepts undercount); P3 add per-account labelling for API customers.
fields.Reference trace: new events 24.4M × 52% = 12.7M automated; precision 0.92 means about 8% of "automated" labels are humans; validation plan: monthly relabelled audit of 1,000 sessions; guardrail: false-positive rate on paying accounts under 1%.
fields.Pump: "Define who is counted before you count."

title: The test says +3% revenue; retention says otherwise

fields.Primer: A short test and a long-term effect disagree / A novelty effect can inflate early results / Defend a ship decision under quarter-end pressure.
fields.Scenario and goal: PM at a subscription product. A four-week pricing-page test shows revenue per user +3.0%; 28-day retention is 36.0% vs 37.2%. Goal: decide whether to ship.
fields.Artifacts: S locked: E1(1) sample 120,000 per arm; E2(2) retention difference SE about 0.2 points (the −1.2 points is statistically clear); revenue lift CI ±1.8%; E3(2) new vs returning users: effect concentrated in new users; E4(2) week-by-week lift: +5.1%, +3.6%, +2.4%, +1.1% (declining); E5(2) projection: if the retention loss persists, six-month revenue = 1.03 × (1 − 1.2/37.2) = 0.997; E6(2) leadership: quarter-end target needs +2%.
fields.Run: Branch 1 interpret → Branch 2 options (ship / extend / ship to 50% with holdout / kill) → PIVOT "Finance offers one more week only" → PROBE "What would you do with a 5% long-term holdout?" → PROBE "What if leadership ships anyway?" → decision rule and stop criteria.
fields.Trap: Short-term tunnel → shipping on revenue alone.
fields.Defensible: P1 extend the test with a 5% long-term holdout and a pre-agreed rule; P2 ship to 50% with kill criteria (accepts risk); P3 redesign the page to avoid the retention loss (accepts delay).
fields.Reference trace: lift decays week by week (novelty effect); retention relative loss 1.2 ÷ 37.2 = 3.2%; 1.03 × 0.968 = 0.997 → about −0.3% if persistent; decision hinges on persistence, so measure it.
fields.Pump: "Project the short-term effect forward with the retention it costs."
fields.Retry seeds: lift decay shape and retention gap.
